extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; merchants and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and normative argument (from Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations) about banking practices (Bank of Amsterdam) and a systematic critique of the mercantilist 'balance of trade' doctrine and related trade restrictions. It explains how banks, receipts, and agio function, and lays out principles for judging trade policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bank price vs. mint price vs. market price (bullion valuation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proportions between the bank price, the mint price, and the market price of bullion are distinct and meaningful: the bank price (credit given for deposits), the mint price (official coinage rate), and the market price (price bullion fetches in the market) differ by measurable spreads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided (Amsterdam, Sept. 1775) show Mexico dollars and various coins quoted at specific guilders per mark; explanation that receipts and bank credits trade at prices reflecting differences between these three prices. Use these three-layer valuations to understand real value and market behavior of deposited bullion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receipts and bank credits are distinct claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The owners of bank credits, and the holders of receipts, constitute two different sorts of creditors against the bank. A receipt entitles the bearer to take out bullion (subject to conditions); bank credit is a ledger claim usable for payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A holder of a receipt cannot draw bullion without re-assigning bank money equal to the deposit price; an owner of bank money cannot take bullion without producing receipts. This separation creates two traded instruments with distinct market values and uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price of receipts and bank money reflects real value differences
rubrics_metrics.description: The holder of a receipt, when purchasing bank money, buys the power of taking out bullion whose mint price is about five percent above the bank price; the owner of bank money, when purchasing a receipt, buys the power to take out bullion whose market price is commonly 2–3 percent above the mint price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore the agio (premium) paid for receipts or bank money is paid for a 'real value' (the right to convert into bullion at a more valuable price), not an imaginary one. Assess prices of these instruments relative to mint and market prices to gauge their fair value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warehouse rent and expiration of receipts produce revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: Receipts are valid for six months and require small keeping charges; receipts that are allowed to expire (fall to the bank) provide the bank with a gain—considered warehouse rent for perpetual keeping of deposits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different metals incur different keeping charges (e.g., higher rent for gold). The bank's income from expired receipts and storage can be a noteworthy revenue stream and explains holders' incentives to let receipts lapse under certain agio conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liquidity and marketability of receipts depends on relative agio
rubrics_metrics.description: Receipts for certain coins (e.g., ducatoons) frequently bring no price in the market when the agio makes taking them out uneconomical; receipts are marketable only when agio/market spreads make withdrawal worthwhile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a receipt will trade by comparing the bank-credit price vs. current coin/bullion market price and factoring keeping charges; receipts may be allowed to expire if cost of withdrawal exceeds market value advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bank policy to cap agio (prevent speculative extremes)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent stock-jobbing between holders of receipts and owners of bank money, the bank resolved to sell bank money at five percent agio and buy it in at four percent agio, keeping the market price perpetually within that band.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A regulated buy/sell spread stabilizes the market price of bank money relative to currency and prevents extreme speculation. This is a concrete institutional rule for maintaining orderly exchange between bank money and circulating coin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bank professes full specie backing for circulating bank money
rubrics_metrics.description: The bank of Amsterdam professes to keep in its repositories, for every guilder for which it gives credit in its books, the value of a guilder either in money or bullion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This full-backing claim is enforced institutionally by annual inspections: new burgomasters visit the treasure, compare it with books, receive it upon oath, and hand it over to successors. Such governance practices are presented as strong guarantees of fidelity and public confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertainty about backing for expired receipts (latent reserves)
rubrics_metrics.description: While the bank surely keeps bullion for all receipts in force, it is less certain whether it likewise retains bullion corresponding to receipts long expired and for which it cannot currently be called upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should note that a portion of bank money may effectively be unclaimed and treated as de facto capital of the bank; but the proportion is supposed small relative to active bank money. This affects assessments of bank solvency in crisis scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingency practice in public calamity (bank run behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: In extreme emergencies (e.g., invasion), when holders of bank money all seek to draw out coin, demand for receipts might spike; the bank, informed by the constitution of its liabilities, would likely break its ordinary rule and pay holders the full perceived value (in money or bullion), plus a couple percent to reconcile values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that in crisis the bank may depart from strict receipt-only payments to prevent disorder—practical crisis-management principle for central institutions with dual instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bank fees, penalties, and other revenue sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The bank levies specific charges: fees on opening accounts and new accounts, transfer fees (with higher discouraging fees for small transfers), penalties for not balancing accounts, overdraft penalty of three percent, warehouse rent, and profit from trading foreign coin that falls to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational revenue is not the bank's original objective (public utility was), but a significant and foreseeable outcome; such fees shape user behavior (discourage many small transfers, encourage balancing) and contribute to institutional sustainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public utility should be primary object of monetary institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Public utility, rather than revenue, was the original object of the bank institution; the revenue which arises from fees and expired receipts was unforeseen and accidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing monetary institutions, prioritize public-service objectives (stability of exchange, convenience) over revenue-maximization; incidental income should not be the driving policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting the balance of trade doctrine (principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of the balance of trade—that a country gains or loses in proportion to deviations from exact equilibrium of gold/silver flows—is false. A natural and voluntary trade between two places is always advantageous to both, even if not equally so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate trade by the gains in exchangeable value of annual produce (increase in annual revenue of inhabitants), not by net flows of precious metals. Policy should not be framed by simplistic ledgering of bullion movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of advantage/gain in trade (metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: By advantage or gain is meant not the increase of quantity of gold and silver, but the increase of the exchangeable value of the annual produce of the land and labour of the country, i.e., increase of annual revenue of inhabitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use increase in exchangeable value and capacity to maintain industry (employment and revenue distribution) as the primary metric when assessing whether a trade is beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of traded goods affects distribution of gains
rubrics_metrics.description: If trade consists of native commodities exchanged mutually, both countries generally gain equally; if one side exports mainly native commodities while receiving foreign goods, the country exporting native commodities gains more (its capital is more directly distributed among its inhabitants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess who benefits from trade by examining whether returns to trade replace capital employed domestically or send revenue abroad (e.g., returns spent on foreign production). Policies should consider distributional effects across inhabitants, not just aggregate totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payments in bullion vs. commodities do not inherently impoverish a nation
rubrics_metrics.description: Payment with gold and silver for imports does not necessarily diminish a nation's capital any more than export of other goods; if foreign purchases bring back goods whose domestic value is higher, the capital and productive capacity of the country can be augmented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat bullion outflows as prima facie evidence of national loss; analyze the domestic value and productive uses of the returns received in exchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct foreign trade of consumption is superior to round-about trade
rubrics_metrics.description: A direct foreign trade of consumption (buying what you want directly from the producer) is always more advantageous than round-about trade (buying through intermediaries or via distant exchanges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing trade relations, favor nearer, more direct exchanges that allow capital to turn over more frequently and maintain more domestic industry per unit of capital employed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free trade benefits the great body of the people; monopoly interests distort policy
rubrics_metrics.description: It is in the interest of the great body of the people to buy whatever they want of those who sell it cheapest; merchants and manufacturers who seek home monopolies distort public judgment and favor protectionist restraints that harm the general welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy evaluation should account for the divergence of interests between small monopoly-seeking groups and the wider public; resist protectionist measures motivated by particular trades' narrow interests rather than public utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wealthy and commercial neighbors are advantageous in peacetime
rubrics_metrics.description: The wealth of neighbouring nations, though dangerous in war, is advantageous in trade because it enables them to exchange to greater value and afford a better market for one's industry; richer neighbours increase domestic employment and revenue via trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade policy should not aim to 'impoverish' neighbours; instead, recognize that prosperous neighbouring markets expand demand for domestic products and benefit most inhabitants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy should not be driven by small self-interested producers' preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Small, underling tradesmen making it a rule to employ chiefly their own customers should not be elevated into national political maxims; the 'sneaking arts' of underling tradesmen produce narrow and harmful trade regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically examine who benefits from proposed trade restraints — avoid codifying narrow producer preferences into national policy when they conflict with broader public advantage.
